body.text: The recent humanitarian operation in Russian-occupied Oleshky, facilitated through diplomatic efforts involving U.S. First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, raised an uncomfortable question for Beijing. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in February 2022, China has pointedly steered clear of any conflict negotiations, but Beijing has emphasized the importance of humanitarian considerations in its response. So why hasn’t China been able to deliver a comparable humanitarian breakthrough in Ukraine?

The temporary ceasefire enabled humanitarian assistance and the evacuation of nearly 800 civilians from Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region. According to the White House, the agreement involved direct negotiations with Russian and Ukrainian representatives, including arrangements for demining, evacuation routes, and medical assistance. It’s proof that even limited negotiations with Russia can produce tangible results.
So why hasn’t Beijing been able to deliver something similar, despite its close strategic relationship with Moscow?

China is capable of mediation, as evidenced by its involvement in other conflicts. Yet while Beijing has repeatedly presented itself as a constructive actor in resolving the Russia-Ukraine war, its diplomatic engagement has produced few results on the ground. China’s limited humanitarian achievements in Ukraine reflect less a lack of diplomatic capacity than a reluctance to use its influence over Russia when doing so might jeopardize a strategically valuable partnership.

The October 23 White House announcement described how the Oleshky operation came about. Melania Trump, acting as “Exclusive Intermediary,” helped Russia and Ukraine come to agreement on “objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms” for the ceasefire.

Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets acknowledged Melania Trump’s role in facilitating the agreement and coordinating between the Ukrainian and Russian negotiators. He also emphasized the importance of maintaining humanitarian cooperation to enable further evacuations and protect civilians.

The agreement offered immediate relief for civilians trapped in dangerous conditions. Nevertheless, it’s far from a durable solution. Oleshky remains under Russian control. The agreement did not require Russia to withdraw its occupying forces, restore Ukrainian administration, or even guarantee the eventual return of displaced residents. Ukrainian officials also accused Russian forces of exploiting the humanitarian pause to rotate troops and transport military supplies. Russia reportedly declined to extend the ceasefire.

For Ukraine, therefore, the value of the Oleshky agreements is limited. Humanitarian relief is valuable, but cannot substitute for the restoration of its sovereignty and territorial integrity, Kyiv’s consistent demands.

Interestingly, despite Beijing’s lack of involvement, the operation received considerable attention in Chinese state media. Xinhua acknowledged Melania Trump’s role and reported on the evacuation of nearly 800 civilians. On November 9, Xinhua also reported President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s allegations that Russian forces had exploited the humanitarian pause to rotate troops and equipment and reinforce their positions in the Kherson region. Another Xinhua analysis published the same day suggested that the humanitarian cooperation achieved in Oleshky could be replicated in other areas of the conflict.

At the November 9 United Nations Security Council meeting on Ukraine, China’s Deputy Permanent Representative Sun Lei welcomed “a localized humanitarian ceasefire, which enabled many civilians to evacuate the frontlines safely and receive humanitarian assistance,” without explicitly naming Oleshky or acknowledging the White House’s mediation role. Sun urged that “humanitarian relief efforts should be intensified.” Yet China has yet to take its own advice by offering to facilitate similar negotiations or implement comparable humanitarian measures.
China’s track record elsewhere proves that Beijing has the diplomatic capability to mediate in overseas conflicts – it’s just choosing not to do so in Ukraine’s case.

In January 2025, China brokered a ceasefire between Myanmar’s military and the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army, an armed group based in eastern Shan State, following negotiations in Kunming. Beijing’s involvement went beyond diplomatic facilitation. China reportedly used economic pressure, including restrictions on border crossings and essential supplies, to influence the MNDAA and an allied armed group. In April, Chinese representatives monitored the ceasefire and witnessed the transfer of the city of Lashio back to Myanmar’s military. Although the arrangement did not resolve Myanmar’s civil war, it demonstrated China’s capacity to combine diplomatic negotiations, economic leverage, and direct monitoring.

Geography helps explain Beijing’s engagement in Myanmar. Andrew Nathan and Andrew Scobell described Chinese foreign policy in terms of “four concentric circles,” with China prioritizing stability along its immediate periphery just after domestic security. Fighting in neighboring Myanmar directly threatens Chinese border security, trade, and investments, creating strong incentives for intervention.

The war in Ukraine doesn’t create the same sense of urgency for China. As Foreign Minister Wang Yi stated in March 2022, “behind the Ukraine crisis is European security.” The direct threat is farther removed from China.

Yet China has also taken a more active mediation role in other conflicts far from its borders. In March 2023, Beijing facilitated the restoration of diplomatic relations between Saudi Arabia and Iran, building on earlier negotiations hosted by Iraq and Oman.

In July 2024, China brought together 14 Palestinian factions, including Fatah and Hamas, producing the Beijing Declaration on Palestinian reconciliation. Although the declaration did not overcome longstanding divisions within the Palestinian cause – much less end the war in Gaza – it demonstrated Beijing’s willingness to pursue diplomatic initiatives beyond its immediate neighborhood.

China’s mediation efforts, then, aren’t dictated by geography alone; strategic interests, available leverage, and simple political will also play crucial roles. In Myanmar, where all four factors combined, China played a direct and impactful mediatory role. Ukraine has not seen the same level of interest, or the same results, in terms of Chinese diplomacy.

China’s relationship with Russia is a big part of the explanation. Beijing enjoys extensive political access to Moscow, with regular summits between the heads of state and government. Russia’s growing dependence on Chinese markets, industrial goods, electronics, and critical supplies also provides potential sources of leverage. Yet leverage becomes effective only when a state is willing to translate its advantages into diplomatic pressure. In Russia’s case, China is simply unwilling to jeopardize a strategic partnership Beijing considers essential in its competition with Washington.

China has limited incentives to pressure Russia over Ukraine, an issue Moscow considers central to its security and territorial ambitions. This does not necessarily mean Beijing benefits from the war’s continuation. Prolonged conflict creates economic uncertainty, strains relations with Europe, and increases scrutiny of Chinese dual-use exports. Nevertheless, China’s diplomatic behavior suggests that preserving strategic cooperation with Russia takes precedence over pursuing breakthroughs that might require Moscow to make concessions. China has shown little public willingness to use either concerted diplomacy or trade leverage to force Russia to the negotiating table.

China’s growing diplomatic activism reflects its ambition to become a major actor in international conflict management. Yet its mediation record reveals a selective approach shaped by strategic interests. In the the case of the Ukraine war, meaningful progress would require Beijing to exercise influence over a strategically important partner. So far, that’s a price China has been unwilling to pay.

The Oleshky evacuation and ceasefire showed that negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow can yield real, if limited, results. China could contribute to similar efforts involving civilian protection, prisoner exchanges, or the return of Ukrainian children. Beijing wouldn’t have to abandon its strategic partnership with Moscow, but it would have to show greater willingness to translate diplomatic declarations urging “humanitarian relief efforts” into action.

Instead, China is loath to put pressure on Russia, even for an outcome as limited as the Oleshky example. Meanwhile, Beijing’s strategic partnership with Moscow limits its credibility as an impartial mediator in Kyiv. China maintains diplomatic engagement with Ukraine, but ties are limited, particularly compared with China’s extensive relationship with Russia.

China’s credibility as a global peace broker will ultimately depend on its ability to bridge the gap between words and deeds. For Ukraine, humanitarian relief is vital, but it cannot replace a settlement based on sovereignty and territorial integrity – principles enshrined in China’s Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence.
